To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we estimate a new angular rotation for the India plate that is significantly different from previous estimates and that the new rotation predicts more rapid plate boundary variations than previous estimates.
we estimated a new angular velocity of the India plate and its contemporary deformation rates from 70 continuous GPS measurements from the plate interior and its seismically-active margins.
the new India-ITR F2008 angular velocity predicts more rapid variations of plate boundary deformation rates than previous estimates and that contemporary deformation rates in India are 1–2mm/yr.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the determination of the angular velocity of the India plate, the estimation of the deformation in the interior of the plate, and the determination of the contemporary deformation along the plate’s boundaries.

the following objectives: (1) to estimate a new angular rotation rate for the India plate, (2) to estimate contemporary intra-plate deformation rates, (3) to estimate deformation rates along India’s seismoactive plate boundaries, (4) to estimate the deformation rates in the Himalaya and Tibet, and (5) to estimate the strain rates in the Indo-Burman Ranges.
the estimation of a new India plate angular velocity and its application to the study of the deformation rates in the India plate and along its boundaries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our new angular velocity is a better fit to GPS velocities than any previous estimate and that the new angular velocity predicts more rapid variations along the India plate boundaries.
the India plate is deforming rapidly and actively at its boundaries and is also deforming internally.
the Indian subcontinent is deforming at ~2 mm/yr, which is consistent with the rate of convergence between India and Eurasia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the new angular velocity and deformation rates for the India plate are more accurate than previous estimates and provide an improved framework for understanding the contemporary deformation of the Indian subcontinent.
India is moving faster than previously estimated and is deforming at a rate of about 3.6 mm/yr at the plate boundaries.
the India-ITRF2014 angular velocity has been significantly improved by the inclusion of GPS data in the western and eastern regions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a more accurate estimate of the angular velocity and a denser GPS network are needed to accurately estimate deformation rates in the interior of the India plate.

India is a rapidly rotating plate, with an estimated Euler pole located in the Indian Ocean, ~1000 km west of Sri Lanka, and with ~3% faster angular velocity than previously estimated, and that this new plate motion model is well suited for studying contemporary deformation along its boundaries.
the India-ITRF 2008 Euler pole should be used in future studies to estimate plate velocities and deformations along its plate boundaries.
